We have evaluated the performance of the proposed model through simulated data and real-world applications, including an examination of time series data related to crime rates in New York City. The SiD detector concept, a proposed detector for the ILC, is a solid-state tracker paired with a high-flux capable calorimeter. Although initially designed for the Large Hadron Electron Collider (LHeC), SiD is now being adapted for the future electron-proton and positron-proton colliders. In this presentation, we will discuss the evolution of the SiD detector design, specifically the sensor layer and the forward part of the calorimeter. The original design featured a thin silicon sensor with a high hit resolution, but it had limitations in photon detection due to its small size. In contrast, the upgraded design features a larger silicon volume in the forward region, improved photon detection capabilities, and a more uniform detector response across different angles. Additionally, the forward part of the calorimeter has been redesigned to reduce material and enhance the detection of low-energy photons and electrons. These upgrades will be highlighted in this presentation. Furthermore, we will present simulation results demonstrating the improved performance of the modified detector design, specifically in photon detection and reconstruction. These results will be presented in the form of simulated data and reconstructed distributions. In the context of the ILC, the modified SiD detector design offers enhanced photon detection capabilities, which will be particularly beneficial for the study of dark photons and axion-like particles. The design's ability to accurately measure low-energy photons and electrons will also contribute to the precise measurement of the W and Higgs boson masses. The presentation will also cover the challenges associated with the large silicon volume in the forward region, including the potential for radiation damage and the detector's overall material budget. The design's material budget is a critical consideration, as it directly impacts the detector's ability to detect low-energy particles. The presentation will conclude with an overview of the R&D activities and prototype development for the modified SiD detector design, as well as the path forward for its construction and integration into the ILC. The Isabelle Archive of Formal Proofs, a comprehensive repository of
proofs in the fields of computer science and mathematics, has been steadily
expanding since its creation in 2013. To guarantee the quality of its
contents, the archive undergoes regular updates and improvements. This process
involves verifying the correctness of existing proofs and reworking them with
the latest version of Isabelle. However, the time and effort required for these
tasks can be substantial, hindering the growth of the archive. To address
this challenge, we present a framework for efficiently demonstrating the
correctness of proofs. This framework streamlines the verification process by
automating the checking of proofs against the latest version of Isabelle and
its underlying mathematical theories. To illustrate the effectiveness of this
approach, we applied the framework to a selection of proofs from the archive,
resulting in a significant reduction in the time and effort needed to verify
their correctness. Furthermore, the framework facilitated the discovery of
errors in previously accepted proofs, underscoring its value in ensuring the
integrity of the archive. To facilitate collaboration and knowledge sharing,
the framework can also be employed to guide novice users through the process
of verifying the correctness of proofs. To achieve this, we incorporated the
framework into a tutorial on the Isabelle proof assistant, which is available

This research introduces a novel 3D pose estimation technique called DeepHMap++ that utilizes only depth images. Unlike conventional methods that employ multiple images or projection techniques, this approach directly utilizes single depth images. DeepHMap++ consists of two primary components: a merged clustering algorithm that uses projection-based methods to group similar 3D data points, and a correspondence learning module that identifies and ranks potential pose candidates. Unlike previous pose estimation methods, DeepHMap++ does not rely on matching 3D models to images, instead using a clustering approach that eliminates the need for precomputed databases. This method was implemented using a convolutional neural network (CNN) and tested using the ModelNet40 dataset, achieving a 0.05 accuracy rate for 24-degree rotations and a 0.06 accuracy rate for 30-degree rotations. Furthermore, DeepHMap++ demonstrated robustness to various lighting conditions and was able to accurately identify poses even with significant occlusions. The foundation theorem is a significant concept in the theory of Coxeter groups, establishing that any element within a Coxeter group can be expressed uniquely as a product of minimal length, comprising the smallest possible number of generators, and can be further broken down into a specific combination of generators from various subgroups of its reflection system. These subgroups, known as foundations, are inherently abstract in nature and are defined by their inherent properties. The foundation theorem classifies all elements within a Coxeter group by identifying their underlying structure, which is essentially a combination of the group's foundations. This thesis aims to expand the foundation theorem to encompass the broader B-type Coxeter groups, which include the Bn, An d Dn. The B-type Coxeter groups encompass two primary forms: the finite Bn, characterized by its n generators, and the affine Bn, defined by its n+1 generators. The foundation theorem has been successfully generalized to apply to both the finite and affine Bn. The approach employed in this thesis is largely analytical, with an emphasis on the interplay between the algebraic and combinatorial aspects of the Coxeter groups. The foundation theorem for the Bn is demonstrated through an explicit formula, which is derived from an innovative presentation of the Chevalley's Theorem. The developed formula is then applied to yield a novel proof for the unitary dual Coxeter orbits theorem, a previously established result. However, neural-based approaches have been observed to struggle with preserving the original n-gram statistics of the training data, which can result in diminished performance when fine-tuning these models for low-resource languages or specific domains. In response to these limitations, we propose a novel residual learning framework that leverages n-gram-based linguistic models to guide the training of neural language models. Our framework consists of two primary components: a neural language model, which generates the final output, and a n-gram-based linguistic model, which generates the residual output. During training, the n-gram-based linguistic model is used to generate the initial prediction, and the neural language model is tasked with producing the residual output. This residual learning approach enables the neural language model to focus on complex tasks, while the n-gram-based linguistic model handles simpler tasks such as word order and part-of-speech tagging. Our proposed framework is particularly effective at preserving the n-gram statistics of the training data, resulting in significant improvements in performance when fine-tuning the models for low-resource languages or specific domains. Reconstructing three-dimensional faces from two-dimensional images is a challenging task, particularly when the images contain low-quality or distorted information. Current deep learning methods often struggle with such difficulties due to their sensitivity to variations in lighting conditions, pose, and occlusions. To address these limitations, we propose a novel approach called Self-Aligned Dual Facial Regression Networks (SADRNet), which utilizes dual networks to simultaneously process two input images and a combined representation of those images. By leveraging self-alignment mechanisms within each sub-network, SADRNet enhances the robustness of its reconstructions by reducing the discrepancies between the two input images and the combined representation. To train this model, we developed a unified training strategy that incorporates both adversarial and cycle-consistency loss functions to achieve high-quality 3D face reconstructions even from images with significant distortions. Experimental evaluations on multiple benchmarks, including the FaceWarehouse dataset and the FFHQ dataset, demonstrate the superiority of SADRNet over existing state-of-the-art methods in terms of reconstruction accuracy and robustness. Notably, our approach achieves exceptional results on datasets that have not been used for training. Code and pre-trained models are available at https://github.com/zhengyuan-yang/SADRNet. Leveraging the ability of SADRNet to generalize across datasets, we successfully applied this model to the challenging task of reconstructing 3D faces from single images, specifically the CelebA-HQ-200k dataset, which resulted in a new dataset called the 3D-CelebA-HQ-200k dataset. This new dataset comprises 200,000 high-quality 3D face reconstructions along with their corresponding texture and landmark maps, which can be accessed at https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1Q8Q8Q8Q8Q8Q8Q8Q8Q8?usp=sharing. To further validate the robustness of SADRNet, we conducted a series of experiments involving face reconstructions from images with occlusions, which demonstrated the model's ability to accurately recover missing facial regions even when occluded by a wide range of objects. To facilitate the evaluation of 3D face reconstruction models on occluded images, we introduced a new benchmark called the OCFAR dataset, which includes 10,000 occluded face images along with their corresponding 3D face reconstructions. This study presents new findings from our previous research on the ionized gas within Seyfert galaxies. We have been analyzing 34 Seyfert galaxies with high signal-to-noise ratios from the CALIFA spectroscopic database, focusing on the ionization patterns of their gas. Our previous work revealed a correlation between the orientation of the galaxy's spiral structure and the direction of its central black hole's ionizing radiation. We have now confirmed the existence of ionized gas outside the axis of ionization, which cannot be explained by standard photoionization models. This discovery challenges our previous understanding of the gas's behavior and suggests that additional processes, such as shock waves, may be present and influencing the gas's ionization. We have developed a new diagnostic tool to detect the presence of shock waves and have applied it to our data, confirming the existence of shock waves in 22 out of 34 Seyfert galaxies. This finding has significant implications for our understanding of the interplay between the central black hole and its host galaxy. We propose that the gas's behavior is more complex than previously thought, with multiple processes, including shock waves, gas outflows, and the host galaxy's star formation, all contributing to the observed ionization patterns. This research has shed new light on the gas's behavior in Seyfert galaxies and has important implications for the study of active galaxies and the growth of their central black holes. It also highlights the need for further research into the gas's behavior in these galaxies. We have made our data and analysis tools available to the research community to facilitate further study of this phenomenon. When training scene flow models using synthetic data, they are typically taught to recognize patterns in metric space. However, real-world scenes differ significantly from these synthetic examples, particularly in terms of density and distribution. As a result, when these models are applied to actual video sequences, they often struggle with extrapolating beyond the learned patterns. This challenge is particularly pronounced in areas with limited training data, such as urban regions, where the model tends to over-rely on neighboring points and fails to consider distant points, leading to inaccurate flow predictions. To address this issue, we propose a novel self-taught scene flow estimation framework that incorporates an adversarial metric training module. This module is designed to learn a feature extractor that maps points to a metric space in which the distribution of real-world scenes is uniform, unlike the distribution of synthetic scenes which is not uniform. By doing so, the model can learn to recognize patterns in a way that is independent of the proximity of points, thus enabling it to accurately estimate scene flow even in areas with limited training data. Our proposed framework significantly outperforms state-of-the-art scene flow estimation methods, including those that use photometric consistency and multi-view constraints, on the KITTI dataset. Notably, it achieves superior performance on urban scenes, demonstrating its robustness and ability to generalize beyond the learned patterns. Our code and models are publicly available at https://github.com/zhengyuan-yang/Adversarial-Metric-Training-for-Scene-Flow.

Indonesia, an archipelago with over 17,000 islands, experiences varying solar time patterns due to its geographical size. This results in significant discrepancies in local time across the country, with some areas differing by as much as 2 hours and 20 minutes from Jakarta time. This discrepancy necessitates the use of sundials with hour lines tailored to specific locations, a practice that has been a part of Indonesian culture for centuries. This tradition is particularly evident in the Javanese calendar, which incorporates a zodiac-based system and utilizes sundials to track time. This paper delves into the history of sundials in Indonesia, specifically in Java, and provides a mathematical framework for calculating the coordinates of sundials. This digital sundial is then simulated using a Java-based programming language, and the results of this simulation are presented along with a discussion on the potential for this technology to be integrated with existing sundials in Indonesia. FNN is based on a unique activation function called the Modulated Cyclic Activation (MCA) function, which is cyclic in nature, similar to the sine activation function, but can be modified to fit any periodic function, allowing it to be trained end-to-end. The conventional SIR model, a fundamental tool for studying the spread of diseases, has a significant limitation: it assumes that each individual infects exactly one other person on average. In reality, some people may infect many others, leading to a significant increase in disease transmission. This research introduces an advanced model that incorporates super-spreader occurrences, where a small number of people infect a large number of others. We demonstrate mathematically that this new model results in a highly contagious epidemic that spreads more quickly, and we provide a precise estimate of its improved transmission rate. Furthermore, we show that even a single super-spreader occurrence can have a substantial impact, potentially delaying the epidemic's recovery by several orders of magnitude. To validate our theoretical findings, we conduct a series of experiments using the new model and a popular real-world dataset, and the results confirm our predictions. Interestingly, we observe that the new model can also produce a non-monotonic behavior, where the recovery time is initially shortened but then lengthened as the number of super-spreader occurrences increases. To gain deeper insights into this phenomenon, we develop a new approach that involves a system of equations, and we show that it accurately captures the dynamics of the epidemic. Finally, we discuss the implications of our research for designing and evaluating random graph models, particularly in the context of epidemic spreading. The new model and the proposed approach can be applied to various scenarios, including social networks, citation networks, and web graphs, and we outline potential research directions for these areas. Our findings indicate that a combination of high learning rates, moderate batch sizes, and high dropout rates can effectively mitigate the negative effects of attacks on deep learning models. To overcome this challenge, we propose a hybrid algorithm called NISQ-HHL that combines Monte Carlo sampling with a shallow quantum circuit for the matrix-vector product. To optimize this hybrid algorithm for maximum benefit, we develop a framework for asset allocation that prioritizes the efficient use of quantum resources. Through simulations, we demonstrate that our framework effectively mitigates noise and increases the accuracy of the Monte Carlo results on a 7-qubit quantum simulator. Furthermore, we apply this framework to a real-world scenario involving the pricing of European call options, and the results indicate that it can lead to substantial improvements in accuracy, with a 4-qubit implementation achieving a 4.5-fold increase in precision over a classical baseline. To further enhance the performance of NISQ-HHL, we introduce a technique called "quantum reweighting" that leverages the capabilities of quantum devices to achieve a 2.5-fold improvement in accuracy with a 4-qubit device. These results demonstrate the potential of NISQ-HHL to accelerate the convergence of Monte Carlo methods on short-term quantum devices. This framework leverages extensive language models through self-supervised learning and a specialized task design. We evaluate DISCO on a newly created dataset of phrasal counterfactuals, demonstrating its superiority over alternative methods and confirming the difficulty of modeling such counterfactuals with current language models. Furthermore, we explore the limitations of DISCO on a second, more challenging dataset of sentence-level counterfactuals, revealing areas for improvement in future work. This research offers a starting point for the study of complex counterfactuals and highlights the potential of extensive language models to capture nuanced aspects of human language and thought. Our findings also reveal that the quality of the extracted labels can be influenced by the quality of the label hierarchy and the relationships between labels, and that there is a clear correlation between the number of extracted labels and the size of the label hierarchy. Our results provide valuable insights into the challenges of multi-label classification and the potential benefits of using a set of labels to describe an instance, and we believe that our proposed method can serve as a foundation for further research in this area. These unique properties can be utilized to create perfect conductors, insulators, and semiconductors, as well as devices that can manipulate and control the flow of electrons and other particles. The accuracy of current computer vision models is significantly impacted by their inability to distinguish between accurate and incorrect predictions, particularly when they fail to account for the context of the entire image. This study focuses on enhancing the context-aware reliability of models in visual association detection tasks. Unlike conventional evaluation methods that solely consider classification accuracy, we employ a more nuanced approach, assessing the performance of models by analyzing both their ability to recognize correct objects within the image and their capacity to differentiate them from incorrect alternatives presented in the same image. Our proposed framework, which incorporates a novel context-aware reliability loss function and a comprehensive evaluation framework, has demonstrated superior performance in various visual association detection benchmarks, including the CUB-200-2011 and the ADE20K datasets. Notably, our results indicate that even subpar models can achieve high context-aware reliability scores when trained with our proposed framework, outperforming state-of-the-art models by a substantial margin. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that the context-aware reliability gap between the best and worst models is substantial, underscoring the need for more rigorous evaluation criteria in visual association detection tasks. Our code and models are publicly available at https://github.com/zhengyuanliu/Reliability-Visual-Association-Detection.

Recent breakthroughs in deep neural networks (DNNs) have achieved remarkable results in various tasks, but their complex nature makes it difficult to understand how they arrive at their conclusions. This lack of transparency is particularly concerning in high-stakes applications, such as self-driving vehicles and medical diagnosis, where the inability to interpret DNN decisions can be detrimental. To address this issue, researchers have been working on developing methods to interpret and explain DNN behavior, but there is a scarcity of studies that investigate the inherent ability of DNNs to learn and generalize information from training data. This study seeks to bridge this knowledge gap by examining how DNNs learn and generalize data, with a focus on understanding their internal workings and representations. We propose a novel approach, called the comprehension framework, which provides a comprehensive framework for comprehending DNN learning and generalization. This framework consists of three primary components: the comprehension module, which assesses the ability of DNNs to learn and generalize data; the representation module, which examines the internal representations of DNNs; and the interpretation module, which evaluates the ability of DNNs to generalize and make predictions based on their internal representations. We also propose a range of methods for evaluating the comprehension, representation, and interpretation of DNNs, including the use of probing tasks, which involve training a separate neural network to extract relevant information from the DNN. We demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed methods by applying them to a range of datasets, including MNIST, CIFAR-10, and ImageNet. Our results indicate that the proposed methods are effective in comprehending the learning and generalization capabilities of DNNs, and provide valuable insights into the internal workings and representations of these networks. We also observe that the ability of DNNs to generalize and make predictions is heavily reliant on the presence of a robust and well-represented label dimension, which is a critical factor in determining the comprehensibility of these networks. Our findings have significant implications for the development of more interpretable and transparent DNNs, and highlight the need for further research into the comprehension, representation, and interpretation of these networks. We believe that our proposed methods and results will serve as a valuable foundation for future research in this area. We also propose a range of open research questions and challenges in the field of DNN comprehension, which we believe are critical to addressing the limitations of these networks and developing more robust and transparent models. We hope that our work will inspire further research into the comprehension, representation, and interpretation of DNNs

This study investigates jet modifications in heavy-ion collisions at the LHC using Monte Carlo simulations with PYTHIA 6.4.22. Jet production is simulated at various scales (100, 500, and 2000 GeV) in both proton-proton and lead-lead collisions. Nuclear PDF sets from EPS09, ABN04, and DRE01 are tested to understand their influence on jet production in nuclear collisions. Additionally, thermal field-theoretical jet production is compared to the equivalent perturbative result. Our analysis reveals that jet data from the LHC are largely insensitive to scale variations, nuclear PDF choices, and thermal corrections, primarily due to the dominance of hard-parton processes over jet production. Consequently, jet spectra in proton-proton collisions remain largely unchanged across different nuclear PDF sets and thermal corrections. In nuclear collisions, the choice of nuclear PDF set significantly impacts jet spectra, with the EPS09 set yielding the highest jet production. Our research highlights the importance of selecting appropriate nuclear PDF sets for interpreting jet data from the LHC, and the limitations of current thermal models in describing jet production in heavy-ion collisions at the LHC. Furthermore, our findings suggest that jet data from the LHC are not yet sensitive to thermal corrections. Our study provides valuable insights for future jet studies at the LHC and other heavy-ion colliders, such as the future Electron-Ion Collider. Our analysis reveals that the discrepancy arises not solely from nonorthogonality, but also stems from the inadequacy of perturbation theory in describing strong interactions between light and matter. This revised formulation offers enhanced flexibility in selecting the basis set, allowing for a more efficient and realistic simulation of strong light-matter interactions. Phylogenetic networks serve as a detailed representation of the evolutionary histories of various species, enabling them to incorporate reticulate evolutionary mechanisms like lateral gene transfer and gene recombination. In contrast to phylogenetic trees, these networks provide a more comprehensive view of the evolutionary process. However, constructing phylogenetic trees from evolutionary data is a well-established task, with numerous efficient algorithms available. In contrast, the task of constructing phylogenetic networks from input data such as trees and the relationships between taxa's genetic material has not been as thoroughly explored. This study introduces a new formal definition for the problem of creating phylogenetic networks and classifies it into three categories based on the type of data provided, before presenting a comprehensive comparison of existing algorithms for this problem. We also present new results on the computational complexity of the problem and its variants, including a polynomial-time algorithm for the most general case when the input data includes any two trees and any transfer scenario. This research aims to provide a clear understanding of the structure of phylogenetic network creators and their connections to related problems, such as tree construction and the breakpoint distance problem. Furthermore, we highlight the potential for further research into the design of efficient algorithms for creating phylogenetic networks. Large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computing relies heavily on error correction, specifically quantum computing's leading approach, surface codes. These codes provide reliable storage by detecting and fixing errors but are limited by their ability to tolerate only a certain level of fault rates. Unfortunately, fault rates in practical applications often surpass this threshold, rendering quantum computing ineffective. To overcome this issue, researchers have proposed using quantum error correction codes in conjunction with classical control systems that detect and respond to errors, a system known as hybrid fault tolerance. This study introduces a new method for generating events that accurately replicate inclusive distributions in LHC collisions, specifically for Pb-Pb collisions at a 2.76 TeV center-of-mass energy. Unlike traditional generator tools, this approach bypasses the complexities of full detector simulations and underlying physics processes, allowing for rapid and cost-effective testing of new physical hypotheses or alternative model parameter settings. Our method involves a straightforward, multi-dimensional comparison of inclusive distributions, including differential distributions of various observables such as transverse momentum, rapidity, and multiplicity. To illustrate the feasibility of this approach, we examine the elliptic flow pattern, a key phenomenon in heavy-ion physics characterized by an anisotropic distribution of particle emissions relative to the reaction plane. Our analysis reveals that the AMPT model effectively captures the elliptic flow behavior in Pb-Pb collisions at 2.76 TeV, both with and without the inclusion of additional particles that influence the reaction. Conversely, we demonstrate that the KOPIK+AMPT model fails to reproduce the observed elliptic flow patterns, thereby highlighting the utility of this event generator method for evaluating the performance of event generators in a rapid and efficient manner. Furthermore, our findings suggest that the KOPIK+AMPT model's inability to replicate the elliptic flow pattern observed in Pb-Pb collisions at 2.76 TeV is not rectified by adjusting the model's parameters to better fit the data. This study provides a valuable framework for the systematic evaluation of event generators, enabling researchers to swiftly assess the performance of new models or parameter settings without the need for extensive simulation simulations. This approach is equally applicable to other heavy-ion colliders, such as the future FAIR and NICA experiments, and can be easily adapted for the study of other phenomena in heavy-ion collisions. These networks exhibit transient characteristics, with nodes forming temporary clusters that dissolve as players quit the game. A phenomenon known as explosive synchronization occurs in complex systems, where a sudden shift from disorder to synchronized behavior is triggered by a minimal increase in connectivity among components. Our study reveals that a specific critical point, identified as the universal exponent alpha, effectively captures the onset of synchronization in various types of oscillator networks. This discovery is further validated through the analysis of real-world networks, where alpha is found to be 1.45+/-0.03. The findings of our research provide a universal framework for studying the onset of explosive synchronization in complex systems. The proposed method is applied to the analysis of real-world networks, including a social network, a biological network, and a transportation network. The entorhinal cortex's grid cell network within the brain's temporal lobe plays a crucial role in navigation by utilizing a unique, periodic mapping system known as grids. At the core of this system are grid neurons, which fire in response to specific spatial patterns, particularly in relation to the periodic structures they form within the brain. These neurons' unique characteristics, including their firing fields, periodic structures, and response to movement, are what enable the brain to create detailed mental maps of its environment, essential for efficient path-finding and location recall. This review aims to summarize the current understanding of grid neurons' properties, including their firing mechanisms, grid periodicity, directional preferences, and responsiveness to head movement, as well as the various theories attempting to explain the underlying mechanisms of this complex navigation system. By examining existing research, this review seeks to provide a comprehensive overview of grid neurons and their role in the brain's navigation network. However, it is essential to note that much remains to be discovered about these intriguing cells, and further research is necessary to fully grasp the intricacies of grid neurons and their involvement in the brain's spatial processing and navigation functions. Concertos and operas from the 18th century hold rich musical history, yet their lyrics remain largely unreadable due to the absence of accurate transcriptions. This project proposes a semi-supervised Convolutive Nonnegative Matrix Factorization technique for automatic lyric extraction from historical audio recordings. Our method leverages a small set of labeled samples to inform a large-scale, unsupervised factorization of the data, resulting in the creation of convolutions and lyric templates that capture recurring patterns. By analyzing these factors, we can identify common structures such as stanza and lyric lengths, and even detect the presence of specific words. Our approach is tested on a dataset of Baroque concertos and demonstrates the ability to accurately transcribe lyrics with minimal supervision. The code and data used in this research are openly available on GitHub. By applying this technique to a Baroque dataset, we can achieve a high level of lyric transcription accuracy with only a single labeled example per song. This achievement is particularly notable given the vast number of under-transcribed Baroque pieces that contain repeating lyrics throughout each song. This research is also relevant to other music transcription applications, such as extracting song titles or identifying specific instruments. Furthermore, this technique can be applied to other domains where patterns repeat over time, such as speech recognition and audio event detection. This connection between mixture models and stochastic geometry and Choquet theory offers a new perspective on the field of mixture modeling and has the potential to contribute to its advancement. The research concludes by outlining potential future directions for object-based programming on GPUs, including the integration of DynaSOAr with parallel programming frameworks and the exploration of other memory allocation algorithms. Deeply supervised autoencoders, specifically those with multiple supervised backbones, have demonstrated impressive performance in various tasks such as semi-supervised learning, transfer learning, and robust learning. However, our analysis uncovers a surprising finding that the features extracted from these deeply supervised autoencoders (DSAs) exhibit both excessive stability and fragility. This paradoxical behavior arises because the features are optimized to minimize both the supervised classification loss and the encoding/decoding reconstruction error simultaneously. This dual objective leads to two undesirable consequences: (1) the features become overly sensitive to minor variations in training data, resulting in poor performance on unlabeled data; (2) the features are excessively stable to significant changes in the training dataset, hindering their ability to generalize to new data. To address these limitations, we introduce an alternative framework called the semi-supervised autoencoder (SSAE) that decouples the classification and reconstruction losses. Specifically, the classification loss is applied only to the encoded features, while the encoding/decoding loss is applied to the input data. This decoupled framework mitigates the excessive stability and fragility issues, enabling it to generalize to both labeled and unlabeled data. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the SSAE framework surpasses the performance of the DSA framework on multiple benchmark datasets. This paper introduces a novel modular system, comprising a robust front-end and a set of lightweight back-end models, and demonstrates its effectiveness in a multi-task reinforcement learning scenario. By utilizing a separate training environment for each back-end model, the system is able to prevent catastrophic interference and achieve superior performance compared to a non-modular model, as confirmed by experiments conducted on a range of complex robotic control tasks. Furthermore, the paper presents a method for efficiently training the back-end models using a technique called "temporally shifted training". This approach allows the system to learn complex temporal patterns and achieve high levels of performance on tasks requiring long-range planning, as evidenced by results obtained on a suite of challenging robotic control benchmarks. The proposed modular system has the potential to significantly advance the field of model-based reinforcement learning by providing a highly versatile and adaptable framework for training high-performance models on complex, real-world tasks. This modular system is highly versatile and can be applied to a wide range of reinforcement learning scenarios, including scenarios involving continuous control, discrete control, and multi-agent reinforcement learning.
